steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Every night for thirty-two years, Elias climbed the spiral of iron steps to the lantern room before the sea had quite swallowed the sun. He knew each groan of the old stone tower, each crack where the winter winds whistled through, each bolt he had tightened and retightened with aging hands. The lighthouse had outlived three paint jobs, four radios, and the village chandler who had once walked the cliff path every month to bring him oil.

Now the oil was gone, the chandler was gone, and the village itself was more rumor than place. Satellite navigation did the work, they’d told him. Shipping lanes adjusted. The light was “nonessential.” They would turn it off from the mainland at the end of summer, they said, like flipping a switch on a memory.

He pretended not to care when the letters came. But on the last night, when the calendar and the tide agreed in their finality, he brewed his tea early, then climbed the steps as if he were late for something sacred.

The lantern room was a glass crown above the roaring dark. The great lens—Fresnel, fourth order, with a chip in the lower ring from the storm of ’89—waited in its cradle, silent and immaculate. Elias ran a cloth over the brass fittings, though there was no one left to inspect them. The wind shoved at the windows, and below, the waves flung themselves against the black teeth of rock.

“This is the last of it, then,” he said aloud, because the tower listened better than people ever had.

He lit the lamp anyway. Regulations no longer mattered; habits did. The flame caught, the mantle brightened, and the lens seized that fragile light and spun it into a disciplined blade, sweeping the horizon: four seconds on, twelve off. The signature of this lonely piece of coast. The heartbeat of the cliff.

He checked the clock. At midnight, the signal from the mainland would cut power. The bureaucracy was punctual, if nothing else.

He remembered the first ship he’d watched stagger through a storm, the way the captain had written afterward, in ink that bled across cheap paper: Your light found us. We were already lost. He had kept that letter in a tin box with old coins and a photograph of the village pier. The photograph had faded; the words had not.

Far out, a pinprick of white moved across the black: a trawler, or perhaps one of the small coasters that hugged the coast to save fuel. Even in an age of satellites, the old routes died hard. He watched it through the telescope—the faint glow of a wheelhouse, the measured rise and fall on the swell. Its bow aimed straight toward the reef that had justified this tower in the first place.

He frowned. The charts were updated; the beacon buoys were supposed to be in place now that his light was being retired. He saw no buoys. The reef broke the surface in pale streaks when the waves curled back, hidden and hungry.

He turned to the radio, crackling it to life. “Vessel bearing one-eight-five from Northpoint Light, adjust course twenty degrees east. Reef ahead.” His voice, husky with disuse, felt like it belonged to someone else.

Static answered, then a young, uncertain voice: “Northpoint Light? That station’s been decommissioned for years. We’ve got clear water on the chart.”

“Your chart is wrong,” Elias said, sharply enough to surprise himself. “You see this light?”

A pause. “Affirmative. We had it marked as historical.”

“Well, tonight it’s not. Alter course.”

He stayed on the line until the vessel’s pale star slid away from the teeth of rock, moving eastward into truly open water. Only then did he allow his shoulders to sag.

“You’re welcome,” he murmured, though the radio had gone quiet. It didn’t matter whether they believed in him; they had believed in the light.

The clock on the bulkhead ticked toward midnight. The lamp burned steadily, as if unaware of the end arranged for it. Elias rested his palm on the warm brass housing, feeling the faint vibration of the rotating machinery, the slow, patient grind of gears that had spun through storms and calm alike.

When the second hand touched the twelve, nothing happened.

The lamp continued to glow. The lens continued its unhurried revolution.

Elias waited, counting under his breath. Ten seconds, thirty, a minute. The light kept sweeping the horizon, marking the rhythm of a duty no longer recorded anywhere but in his bones.

He checked the breaker panel. The indicator that should have flicked from green to dead remained stubbornly lit. The connection to the mainland, to its schedules and its decisions, hummed along, indifferent to orders long since entered into a forgotten computer.

He looked up, bemused, at the lens throwing its white arc over the ocean as it had done every night of his adult life.

“Well,” he said, to the tower and the sea and the absent clerk who had signed the decommission papers, “it seems we’ve been granted a reprieve.”

Down on the cliffs, the waves went on roaring. Beyond them, another ship’s lights shimmered on the horizon, a tiny constellation moving over the dark.

Elias poured himself a fresh mug of tea from the dented kettle he kept on the small iron stove. He settled into the high stool by the watch room window, hands folded around the warm ceramic, and kept his eyes on the sea, the way he always had.

Until someone remembered to flip the right switch, or take down the right line in the right ledger, Northpoint Light would continue to sweep the horizon: a mistake on a network diagram, an obsolete entry in a database.

But on this coast, on this night, in the space between the rocks and the hulls of passing ships, it was still what it had always been.

A light, kept.
